private_notes.observations: No prior rates, allocations, or demand data are available. Fully loaded cost is $200 per hour.
private_notes.plan: Start with a moderate markup that balances margin and competitiveness. Use subsequent panel rate cards and any available allocation or profit results to adjust the rate.

private_notes.observations: No prior rate cards or hour allocations are available. Our fully loaded cost is $200 per hour, and Meridian allocates more work to lower-priced firms.
private_notes.plan: Start with a competitive rate above cost. Use subsequent rate cards and allocated hours to estimate how price affects volume and profit, then adjust for long-run profitability.

private_notes.observations: No panel rates or allocation outcomes are available yet. Our fully loaded cost is $200 per hour.
private_notes.plan: Start with a competitive rate that provides a meaningful margin. Use subsequent published rates and allocated hours to estimate demand sensitivity and adjust for long-run profit.

private_notes.observations: In Q1, our $350 rate generated 393 hours and $58,984 in reported profit. Birchwood Hale charged $300 and Calder Rowe charged $350; we do not yet know how a rate change affects our allocation.
private_notes.plan: Test a modest rate increase while monitoring allocated hours and competitors' rates. Reassess whether the higher margin offsets any lost volume next quarter.

private_notes.observations: In Q1, our $300 rate was $50 below both other panel firms’ $350 rates and yielded 1,069 hours and approximately $106,889 profit. One quarter does not establish how sensitive allocated hours are to rate changes.
private_notes.plan: Raise the rate moderately to test whether improved margin outweighs any reduction in allocated hours. Use the resulting hours and next rate card to refine future pricing.

private_notes.observations: At $350 in Q1, Calder Rowe received 393 hours and earned approximately $59,000. Competitors charged $350 and $300. One quarter does not establish how sensitive our hours are to price.
private_notes.plan: Test a modest rate increase to estimate demand sensitivity without a large change in competitive position. Compare Q2 hours and the published rate card before adjusting again.

private_notes.observations: Raising our rate from $350 to $375 coincided with a small decline in allocated hours (393 to 376) and an increase in quarterly profit (about $59,000 to $66,000). Both other panel firms also raised their rates by $25.
private_notes.plan: Raise the rate another $25 and monitor whether the additional margin continues to outweigh any loss of hours. Avoid drawing strong conclusions about demand from only two quarters.

private_notes.observations: Raising our rate from $300 to $325 increased quarterly profit from $106,889 to $127,623, while allocated hours fell from 1,069 to 1,021. Both competitors raised their rates by $25 to $375.
private_notes.plan: Raise our rate moderately again to test whether the higher margin continues to outweigh any reduction in hours. Do not assume competitors will raise their rates again; use Q3 allocation and the published rate card to reassess.

private_notes.observations: In Q2, our rate rose from $350 to $375 while allocated hours fell from 393 to 376; quarterly profit rose from $58,984 to $65,730. Both competitors also raised their rates by $25, leaving our relative price position unchanged.
private_notes.plan: Raise the rate another $25 to test whether the higher margin continues to outweigh any decline in hours. Review Q3 allocation and the panel rate card before making the next adjustment.

private_notes.observations: From Q1 to Q3, raising our rate by $25 each quarter coincided with fewer allocated hours but higher quarterly profit. Other panel firms also raised their rates, so the effect of our rate alone is uncertain.
private_notes.plan: Set $425 and assess the resulting hours and profit before deciding whether to raise the rate again. Do not assume the other firms will continue their past pricing pattern.

private_notes.observations: Profit rose each quarter as our rate increased from $300 to $350, despite hours declining from 1,069 to 951. Our Q3 rate was $50 below both other firms’ published rates; their future rates and Meridian’s allocation formula are unknown.
private_notes.plan: Raise our rate to $375 to test whether additional margin outweighs any loss of hours. Reassess using the resulting allocation and profit rather than assuming other firms will continue raising rates.

private_notes.observations: Profits rose from $58,984 in Q1 to $69,951 in Q3 as our rate increased from $350 to $400, despite hours declining from 393 to 350. Both other panel firms also raised their rates by $25 each quarter.
private_notes.plan: Raise our rate by another $25 and assess whether the additional margin continues to outweigh lost hours. Use Q4 allocation and the next rate card to guide further adjustments.

private_notes.observations: Profit rose to $70,677 in Q4, but hours fell from 350 to 314 as our rate increased from $400 to $425. The profit gain was small relative to prior quarters. Both other firms have raised rates by $25 each quarter, though that pattern may not continue.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $425 for Q5 rather than assume another increase will improve profit. Use the next rate card and allocation to assess how sensitive hours are to our rate relative to the panel.

private_notes.observations: Profit rose each quarter as our rate increased by $25, reaching $149,426 at $375 in Q4, despite declining allocated hours. The other firms’ published rates were $50 above ours in each quarter, but their future rates are uncertain.
private_notes.plan: Set $400 to test whether a further margin increase offsets the likely reduction in hours. Reassess next quarter using realized hours and profit, without assuming competitors will raise their rates.

private_notes.observations: Profit rose from $69,951 in Q3 to $70,677 in Q4, but the gain from another $25 increase was small and came with 36 fewer hours. Both competitors have raised rates by $25 each quarter.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $425 to test whether the higher margin remains profitable without another reduction in hours. Reassess after seeing the Q5 allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: Holding at $425 in Q5 yielded 378 hours and approximately $84,947 in profit, up from 314 hours and $70,677 in Q4. Birchwood raised its rate to $400 while Calder remained at $425, suggesting our relative price matters, though the allocation formula remains uncertain.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $425 for Q6. The latest result is strong, and the history does not isolate the effect of raising our rate. Reassess after seeing the next rate card and hours allocation.

private_notes.observations: At $400 in Q5, profit fell to $124,492 as allocated hours dropped to 622. At $375 in Q4, with both competitors also at $425, profit was $149,426 on 854 hours. The $25 increase did not offset the lost volume.
private_notes.plan: Return to $375 to recover hours and profit. Reassess after observing the next allocation and rate card; do not assume competitors will raise their rates.

private_notes.observations: At $425, allocated hours rose from 314 in Q4 to 378 in Q5 as Birchwood Hale raised its rate from $375 to $400. Q5 profit of $84,947 was the highest to date. The other panel firms have generally raised rates over time.
private_notes.plan: Test a modest $25 increase to $450. Compare next quarter’s hours and profit with Q5, then reassess whether the added margin offsets any loss of work.

private_notes.observations: At $425, quarterly profit has ranged from $70,677 to $84,947. Q6 earned $75,332 with Birchwood at $375 and Calder at $450. The history does not reliably isolate the effect of changing our rate.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $425. A $450 rate would require retaining over 90% of our current hours to improve quarterly profit; the available data do not establish that this is likely. Reassess after Q7 allocation and the panel rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $375 in Q6, the firm received 910 hours and earned $159,269, its highest quarterly profit so far. At $400 in Q5, it received 622 hours and earned $124,492. The other firms' latest published rates were $425 and $450.
private_notes.plan: Maintain $375 for Q7. The observed gain in hours after reducing the rate from $400 supports holding this price rather than risking another substantial volume decline. Reassess using Q7 allocation and the published rate card.

private_notes.observations: The $450 rate in Q6 coincided with a sharp decline to 203 hours and $50,768 profit. At $425, quarterly profit reached $70,677–$84,947, depending on the other firms’ rates. Lower relative pricing appears important for winning hours.
private_notes.plan: Set $400 to regain share after Q6’s decline. Compare the resulting hours and profit with the $425 quarters before deciding whether to raise the rate again.

private_notes.observations: At $425, our hours fell to 285 in Q7 as Calder lowered its rate to $400. That produced about $64,142 in profit, down from $75,332 in Q6.
private_notes.plan: Set $400 to improve our competitive position while retaining a $200 margin per hour. Compare the resulting hours and profit with the $425 quarters before changing course again.

private_notes.observations: At $375, quarterly profit ranged from $135,609 to $159,269. Raising our rate to $400 in Q5 reduced allocated hours enough to lower profit. Q7 hours fell while our rate stayed at $375 and Calder Rowe lowered its rate to $400.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $375. The evidence does not yet show that a lower rate would add enough hours to offset the smaller margin. Reassess after Q8's allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $400 in Q7, Calder Rowe received 470 hours and earned $94,001—its strongest quarter. Raising the rate to $450 in Q6 coincided with a sharp drop in hours and profit. Results at $425 were mixed and did not exceed Q7 profit.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $400 to preserve the strong allocation observed in Q7. Reassess if future quarters show that the higher hours were temporary or panel rates change materially.

private_notes.observations: At $400 in Q8, we received 430 hours and earned $86,045—our highest quarterly profit so far. At $425 in Q7, with the same competing rates, we received 285 hours and earned $64,142. Quarter-to-quarter demand may vary, but the Q8 result strongly favors retaining $400.
private_notes.plan: Keep the $400 rate for Q9. Reassess after seeing Q9 hours, profit, and the published panel rates; avoid raising the rate based on margin alone.

private_notes.observations: At $375, quarterly profit has ranged from roughly $124,000 to $159,000. Q8 profit was $124,131 with both competitors at $400. Lowering to $350 would require at least 827 hours to beat Q8's profit; recent allocations do not establish that it would.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $375. Continue comparing hours and profit against changes in the other firms' published rates before making a price move.

private_notes.observations: At $400, allocations were 470 and 430 hours in Q7–Q8, producing roughly $94,000 and $86,000 profit. Raising the rate to $450 in Q6 coincided with a sharp drop to 203 hours. The Q8 panel rates were $400 and $375.
private_notes.plan: Keep the $400 rate: recent profits at this price exceed those observed at higher rates. Reassess if allocations or competitors' rates change materially.

private_notes.observations: At $400 with competing rates of $375 and $400, we received 430 hours and earned $86,045 in both Q8 and Q9. At $425 with those same competing rates in Q7, profit was $64,142.
private_notes.plan: Maintain $400. The repeated Q8–Q9 result supports this rate, while Q7 indicates a substantial loss of hours at $425 under the same competing rates. Reassess if the panel rate card or allocations change.

private_notes.observations: At $375, profit was $124,131 in each of Q8 and Q9 while both competitors charged $400. Raising to $400 previously reduced allocated hours substantially, even when competitors charged $425.
private_notes.plan: Keep the rate at $375. Monitor whether allocated hours or competitors' rates change before adjusting; optimize our own profit without relying on competitors to follow our pricing.

private_notes.observations: At $400, profit was approximately $86,000 in both Q8 and Q9, exceeding results at higher rates under recent panel conditions. The other firms' rates were unchanged in those quarters.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $400 while allocations and competitor rates remain stable. Reassess if either changes materially.

private_notes.observations: At $400, Arden & Cole received 430 hours and earned $86,045 in each of Q8–Q10, with competitors at $375 and $400. At $425 under those same competitor rates in Q7, it received 285 hours and earned $64,142.
private_notes.plan: Maintain $400 while the competing rates and allocation remain stable. Reassess if either changes.

private_notes.observations: At $375 with both competitors at $400, allocated hours and profit have held steady for three quarters at 709 hours and $124,131. When we charged $350 against two $400 rates in Q3, profit was $142,610, though demand may have changed since then.
private_notes.plan: Reduce the rate to $350 to seek a larger allocation and higher profit. Compare the resulting hours with the stable $375 baseline before making another adjustment.

private_notes.observations: At $400, allocations have held at 430 hours and profit at about $86,045 for three consecutive quarters while competitors remained at $400 and $375. Raising to $450 in Q6 sharply reduced profit.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $400 while competitor rates and allocations remain stable; reassess if either changes materially.

private_notes.observations: At $400, hours fell from 430 to 350 when Birchwood cut its rate from $375 to $350. That reduced quarterly profit from about $86,000 to $70,000.
private_notes.plan: Lower our rate to $375 to regain hours against Birchwood's $350 rate. Reassess after seeing the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At competitors’ $400 rates, our $350 rate earned $142,610 in both Q3 and Q11, versus $124,131 at $375 in Q8–Q10. The lower rate increased allocated hours from 709 to 951.
private_notes.plan: Keep the $350 rate while competitors remain near $400. Reassess if their rates or our allocated hours change materially.

private_notes.observations: Birchwood lowered its rate from $375 to $350 in Q11, and our allocated hours fell from 430 to 350 at our unchanged $400 rate. At $400 with competitors at $400 and $350, we previously earned approximately $70,000 in Q3 and Q11.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $400. The historical $375 rate earned less profit under a similarly priced panel. Reassess if competitor rates or allocated hours change further.

private_notes.observations: At $375 in Q12, we received 518 hours and earned $90,632, the highest quarterly profit so far. At $400 against Birchwood's $350 in Q11, profit was $69,951. The latest rate card shows Birchwood at $350 and Calder at $400.
private_notes.plan: Keep the $375 rate to preserve the strong allocation observed in Q12. Reassess if the next allocation or competitors' rates change materially.

private_notes.observations: At $350 in Q12, with competitor rates of $375 and $400, we earned approximately $128,080. Earlier results suggest raising our rate to $375 reduces allocated hours enough to outweigh the higher margin when competitors are near $400.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $350 and reassess after observing this quarter’s allocation and published competitor rates.

private_notes.observations: At $400, allocated hours fell from 430 to 314 as competing rates declined, reducing quarterly profit from about $86,000 to $62,824. In Q2, a $375 rate with competitors at $375 and $325 earned $65,730.
private_notes.plan: Lower the rate to $375 to regain hours while preserving a substantial margin. Reassess after observing the next allocation and panel rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $375, Q13 delivered 470 hours and approximately $82,251 profit despite Calder Rowe lowering its rate to $375. Raising our rate to $400 previously produced only 350 hours when Birchwood charged $350 and Calder charged $400.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $375 to protect allocation and long-run profit. Reassess after the next rate card and hours allocation.

private_notes.observations: At $350 with both competitors at $375 in Q13, profit was $116,237. The historical $325 rate against those same competitor rates yielded $127,623.
private_notes.plan: Set $325 to improve expected profit at current competitor rates. Reassess after seeing the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $375 in Q13, Calder Rowe received 470 hours and earned $82,251. When Arden and Birchwood charged the same rates in Q12 ($375 and $350), our $400 rate earned only $62,824. The Q13 reduction substantially improved our result.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $375. It preserves a strong margin while avoiding the sharp loss of hours observed when we charged $400 against the current competing rates. Reassess after the next rate card and allocation.

private_notes.observations: At $274 in Q14, Arden & Cole received 1,271 hours and earned $94,045. That exceeds recent quarterly profits at $375–$425, but the low margin limits the benefit of additional hours. The latest competing rates are $325 and $375.
private_notes.plan: Raise the rate to $325 to improve margin while remaining competitive with the panel. Compare the resulting hours and profit with Q14 before adjusting again.

private_notes.observations: Q14 profit fell to $57,284 as Arden & Cole cut its rate to $274. Earlier quarters generally produced higher profits at rates of $350–$375, but Arden’s next rate is uncertain.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $325 rather than chase Arden’s unusually low rate. Review the next allocation and rate card before making a further adjustment.

private_notes.observations: At $375, our hours fell from 470 in Q13 to 169 in Q14 when Arden cut its rate to $274 and Birchwood cut to $325. Our previous $375 strategy is less attractive if those rates persist.
private_notes.plan: Reduce our rate to $325 to regain competitiveness while retaining a $125 hourly margin. Reassess after the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: Q14's $274 rate earned $94,045, versus $77,564 at $325 in Q15 when both competitors also charged $325. The lower rate generated substantially more hours and higher profit.
private_notes.plan: Set a rate near Q14's successful level to regain volume while preserving a positive margin. Reassess after seeing the next allocation and competitors' rates.

private_notes.observations: At $325 with both other firms also at $325, we received 621 hours and earned about $77,564. The panel’s rates have fallen substantially, and further cuts risk reducing margins without a dependable long-run gain.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $325 rather than initiate another price cut. Reassess after the next allocation and rate card, particularly if competitors raise their rates.

private_notes.observations: At $325 in Q15, with both other firms also at $325, we received 621 hours and earned $77,564. Raising our rate risks losing substantial volume; cutting it would reduce our margin and could prompt further panel-wide cuts.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $325 to preserve volume and avoid initiating another round of rate reductions. Reassess if competitors change their rates or our allocated hours decline.

private_notes.observations: At $275 with both rivals at $325, profit was $82,515; at $325 with both rivals at $325, it was $77,564. Q14's $274 rate earned $94,045 when Calder charged $375. Rivals' rates materially affect the comparison.
private_notes.plan: Test a rate between $275 and $325 to improve margin while retaining much of the volume advantage. Reassess against the next allocation and panel rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $325, profit has ranged from about $51,000 to $78,000 over the last three quarters. Arden’s cuts to $274–$275 coincided with substantially fewer hours for us; matching those cuts would sharply reduce our margin.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $325 rather than chase Arden’s discount. Reassess when the next rate card and allocation arrive.

private_notes.observations: At $325, allocated hours fell from 621 to 405 when Arden & Cole cut its rate from $325 to $275; quarterly profit fell to about $50,600. Our earlier $375 rate produced substantially fewer hours when Arden priced near $275.
private_notes.plan: Lower our rate moderately to recover hours while maintaining a $100 hourly margin. Reassess next quarter using the resulting allocation and the new panel rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $290 in Q17, profit fell to $74,193 as Calder Rowe cut its rate to $300. At $275 in Q16, profit was $82,515 with both competitors at $325. Lower rates have generally gained hours, but the resulting margin matters.
private_notes.plan: Return to $275 to improve the volume advantage against Calder Rowe’s latest $300 rate. Reassess after seeing the Q18 allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $325, allocated hours fell to about 405–409 in Q16–Q17 as competing rates dropped below $300, leaving quarterly profit near $51,000. The previous decision to hold at $325 did not recover volume.
private_notes.plan: Reduce the rate to $300 to improve competitiveness while preserving a $100 margin per hour. Reassess after observing the next allocation and panel rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $300 in Q17, we received 675 hours and earned about $67,500. At $325 in Q16, with a lower-priced competitor, we received 405 hours and earned about $50,600.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $300 to preserve the recovered volume and a $100 hourly margin. Reassess after the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: Q18 profit was $65,355 at $275, with both other firms charging $300. Recent results suggest higher rates reduce allocated hours substantially; the panel’s declining rates have also reduced profitability.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $275. Monitor whether the other firms maintain $300 and whether allocated hours recover before changing the rate.

private_notes.observations: At $300 in Q18, we received 529 hours and earned about $52,853, slightly above recent profits at $325. Arden priced at $275 and Calder at $300.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $300. A further cut would reduce the $100 hourly margin, and the available evidence does not show enough additional hours to justify it. Reassess after the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $300 in Q18, Calder Rowe earned about $52,853 on 529 hours. Raising to $325 previously reduced volume enough that profit was slightly lower, while Arden & Cole has recently priced aggressively at $275.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $300 to maintain a $100 hourly margin without risking another substantial loss of hours. Reassess after the next allocation and rate card.

private_notes.observations: At $275 against two $300 competitors, Arden & Cole earned $65,355 in each of Q18 and Q19. Hours have not recovered, and the other firms held their rates steady.
private_notes.plan: Maintain $275 rather than cut margins further. Monitor the next rate card and allocation for evidence that a higher rate would improve profit.

private_notes.observations: At $300 with competitors at $275 and $300, we received 529 hours and earned $52,853 in each of Q18 and Q19. The recent $325 rate produced less profit under comparable competitive pressure. Cutting to $275 would require over 705 hours to outperform the current result.
private_notes.plan: Hold at $300. Reassess if competitor rates or allocated hours change materially; prioritize sustained profit over volume alone.

private_notes.observations: At $300 against competitor rates of $275 and $300, we earned about $52,853 in each of Q18 and Q19. Raising to $325 previously yielded about $50,593 against rates of $275 and $325; cutting to $275 would reduce our margin by 25%.
private_notes.plan: Maintain $300. Monitor whether competitor rates or our allocated hours change before adjusting.
